payload.name: superior-pharyngeal-constrictor
payload.scope: People made the superior-pharyngeal-constrictor construct to map the uppermost pharyngeal constrictor muscle band that forms the posterior and lateral walls of the superior pharynx, enabling clinicians to localize pharyngeal constriction defects and retropharyngeal abscesses.

definition.body: The superior pharyngeal constrictor is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the quadrate sheet of muscle forming the uppermost band of the posterior and lateral walls of the pharynx. Parameters: (1) the origins - pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe (shared with the buccinator), and the medial pterygoid plate of the sphenoid bone; (2) the insertion - the pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone and the pharyngeal raphe, a midline tendon where the fibers of both sides interdigitate; (3) the fiber orientation - lower fibers run inferiorly, upper fibers overlap the middle constrictor; (4) the aperture - the stylopharyngeus nerve passes through between the superior and middle bands; (5) the clinical significance - landmark for pharyngeal surgery, origin of superior constrictor palsy in stroke, and site of pharyngoplasty for velopharyngeal insufficiency. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, otolaryngology references, and swallowing assessment protocols. e.g.: the superior pharyngeal constrictor in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition by Drake; the pharyngeal raphe during constrictor repair in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; stylopharyngeus nerve passing through the constrictor in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition | not: the middle-pharyngeal-constrictor (the intermediate band arising from the hyoid bone, a distinct muscle layer); the inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor arising from the cricoid and thyroid cartilages, a distinct muscle layer; the buccinator (the facial muscle sharing the pterygomandibular raphe, not a pharyngeal muscle) [formal: constrictor pharyngis superior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The middle pharyngeal constrictor is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the fan-shaped sheet of muscle forming the intermediate band of the posterior and lateral walls of the pharynx. Parameters: (1) the origins - the lesser and greater horns of the hyoid bone and the hyoidothyroid ligament; (2) the insertion - the pharyngeal raphe and overlapping fibers posteriorly where it fuses with the superior constrictor above and the inferior constrictor below; (3) the fiber arrangement - fibers fan superiorly to overlap the superior constrictor and inferiorly to be overlapped by the inferior constrictor; (4) the aperture - the stylopharyngeus muscle passes between the superior and middle constrictors, and the glossopharyngeal nerve and tonsillar artery pass between the middle and inferior constrictors; (5) the clinical significance - landmark in tonsillectomy (the constrictor is the bed from which the tonsil is dissected), site of pharyngeal diverticula, and reference for pharyngeal pacing. Parameters: (1) the origin — apex of the styloid process and its associated stylohyoid ligament; (2) the course — descends along the lateral pharyngeal wall, passing between the superior and middle constrictor muscles to insert into the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage; (3) the innervation — glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), the only pharyngeal muscle with this innervation; (4) the action — elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and speech, widens the pharyngeal cavity; (5) the clinical significance — landmark in tonsillectomy surgery, its atrophy assessed in glossopharyngeal nerve palsy, and its course relevant to transstyloid surgical approaches to the parapharyngeal space. definition.body: The palatopharyngeus muscle is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the paired longitudinal muscle of the pharynx originating from the soft palate, whose fibers descend to merge with the salpingopharyngeus and insert into the posterior border of the thyroid cartilage, elevating the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and forming the posterior tonsillar pillar. Parameters: (1) the origin — the palatopharyngeal aponeurosis from the posterior border of the soft palate (palatine aponeurosis); (2) the course — descends along the lateral pharyngeal wall as a muscular band; (3) the fusion — merges with the salpingopharyngeus muscle superiorly; (4) the insertion — posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and the pharyngeal wall; (5) the clinical significance — forms the palatopharyngeal fold (posterior tonsillar pillar) visible on oropharyngeal inspection, its function impaired in velopharyngeal insufficiency. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in head-and-neck anatomy, otolaryngology, and swallowing assessment. e.g.: palatopharyngeus described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition as part of the palatopharyngeal complex; palatopharyngeal fold visualized on oral examination as the posterior tonsillar pillar; palatopharyngeus weakness assessed in velopharyngeal dysfunction per Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the salpingopharyngeus-muscle (the superior muscle that blends with it, originating from the auditory tube); the levator-veli-palatini (a separate soft palate muscle originating from the temporal bone, innervated differently); the tensor-veli-palatini (another soft palate muscle not part of the longitudinal pharyngeal muscle group) [formal: musculus palatopharyngeus | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: palatine-tonsil
payload.scope: People made the palatine-tonsil construct to map the paired lymphoid tissue masses embedded in the lateral walls of the oropharynx, so that clinicians can diagnose tonsillitis, distinguish normal lymphoid tissue from neoplasia, and plan tonsillectomy.

definition.body: The palatine tonsil is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired oval masses of lymphoid tissue located in the tonsillar fossa between the palatoglossal and palatopharyngeal arches at the junction of the oral cavity and oropharynx. Parameters: (1) the location — bilateral tonsillar fossae bounded anteriorly by the palatoglossal arch (palatoglossus muscle) and posteriorly by the palatopharyngeal arch (palatopharyngeus muscle) in the lateral oropharyngeal wall; (2) the lymphoid architecture — a central core of lymphoid follicles with germinal centers, covered by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium that invaginates to form 10–20 crypts; (3) the blood supply — tonsillar branch of the facial artery as the principal supply, with contributions from the ascending palatine artery, dorsal lingual arteries, and descending palatine artery; (4) the innervation — glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via tonsillar branches for sensory innervation and the tonsillar plexus, plus the lesser palatine nerves; (5) the clinical significance — common site of bacterial colonization (Group A Streptococcus), recurrent tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess formation, and tonsillar hypertrophy causing obstructive sleep apnea. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in otolaryngology, head and neck surgery, and clinical examination. e.g.: the palatine tonsil as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; tonsillectomy specimen showing lymphoid follicles and crypt architecture on histology per Bailey's Head and Neck Surgery; tonsillar hypertrophy grading on lateral neck radiograph used in pediatric sleep apnea assessment | not: the lingual-tonsil (the lymphoid tissue at the base of the tongue, a distinct mass); the nasopharyngeal-tonsil (adenoid, lymphoid tissue in the nasopharynx, a separate structure); the tubal-tonsil (Gerlach's tonsil, lymphoid tissue near the Eustachian tube opening) [formal: tonsilla palatina | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

definition.body: The bronchiole is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the terminal branches of the conducting airways within the lung parenchyma, distal to the terminal bronchioles, that continue air conduction toward the alveolar gas-exchange units. Parameters: (1) the caliber — diameters ranging from approximately 1 mm in the larger bronchioles to less than 0.5 mm, decreasing distally through successive generations (Weibel model generation 14-23); (2) the wall architecture — walls composed of smooth muscle and elastic fibers without cartilage plates or submucosal glands, lined by simple cuboidal epithelium in terminal bronchioles transitioning to simple squamous in respiratory bronchioles; (3) the mucociliary apparatus — ciliated cells and Clara (club) cells secreting surfactant proteins and protease inhibitors, with diminishing ciliated surface area distally; (4) the bronchial smooth muscle — circularly arranged smooth muscle forming a thicker proportion of the wall relative to diameter, regulating airflow through bronchoconstriction and bronchodilation; (5) the respiratory division — respiratory bronchioles as transitional structures with scattered alveoli budding from their walls, marking the onset of gas exchange within the conduction pathway. definition.body: The alveolus is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the microscopic thin-walled air sac within the lung parenchyma where oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse between the air and the pulmonary capillary blood. definition.body: The pleura is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the double-layered serous membrane that envelops the lungs and lines the thoracic cavity, creating a closed potential space whose thin fluid layer enables frictionless respiratory movement. Parameters: (1) the two layers — the visceral pleura adhering directly to the lung surface including the interlobar fissures, and the parietal pleura lining the thoracic wall, divided into costal (rib-facing), diaphragmatic (diaphragm-facing), mediastinal (midline), and cervical (cupula) regions; (2) the pleural cavity — the potential space between the visceral and parietal layers containing approximately 10-20 mL of serous fluid, maintaining negative intrapleural pressure essential for lung expansion; (3) the pleural reflection lines — anatomical lines where the parietal pleura transitions between regions, forming recesses (costodiaphragmatic and costomediastinal) that allow lung expansion during deep inspiration; (4) the blood supply — visceral pleura supplied by bronchial arteries, parietal pleura supplied by intercostal and internal thoracic arteries, with venous drainage following arterial patterns; (5) the innervation — parietal pleura innervated by somatic nerves (intercostal nerves for costal and diaphragmatic pleura, phrenic nerve for mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura), visceral pleura innervated by autonomic fibers with no pain sensation. Parameters: (1) the two layers — the visceral pleura adhering directly to the lung surface including the interlobar fissures, and the parietal pleura lining the thoracic wall, divided into costal (rib-facing), diaphragmatic (diaphragm-facing), mediastinal (midline), and cervical (cupula) regions; (2) the pleural cavity — the potential space between the visceral and parietal layers containing approximately 10-20 mL of serous fluid, maintaining negative intrapleural pressure essential for lung expansion; (3) the pleural reflection lines — anatomical lines where the parietal pleura transitions between regions, forming recesses (costodiaphragmatic and costomediastinal) that allow lung expansion during deep inspiration; (4) the blood supply — visceral pleura supplied by bronchial arteries, parietal pleura supplied by intercostal and internal thoracic arteries, with venous drainage following arterial patterns; (5) the innervation — parietal pleura innervated by somatic nerves (intercostal nerves for costal and diaphragmatic pleura, phrenic nerve for mediastinal and central diaphragmatic pleura), visceral pleura innervated by autonomic fibers with no pain sensation. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in radiology, thoracic surgery, and pulmonary medicine. e.g.: the pleura as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; pleural effusion visualized as blunting of the costodiaphragmatic recess on upright chest radiograph; thoracentesis procedure performed under ultrasound guidance per American College of Chest Physicians guidelines | not: the pleural-cavity (the potential space between the two layers of pleura, a distinct structure); the costal-pleura (the parietal pleura lining the ribs, a regional substructure) [formal: pleura | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

payload.name: lung
payload.scope: People made the lung construct to map the paired respiratory organs of gas exchange within the thoracic cavity, so that clinicians can diagnose pulmonary disease, interpret chest imaging, and manage respiratory failure.

definition.body: The lung is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired spongy respiratory organs within the thoracic cavity, separated by the mediastinum, in which air is conducted through branching bronchi to alveolar gas-exchange surfaces. Parameters: (1) the lateralization — the right lung (three lobes: upper, middle, and lower, separated by the oblique and horizontal fissures) and the left lung (two lobes: upper and lower, separated by the oblique fissure, with the lingula corresponding to the right middle lobe); (2) the bronchial tree — the hierarchical branching from the main bronchi through lobar, segmental, and subsegmental bronchi to bronchioles and respiratory bronchioles, with cartilage decreasing and smooth muscle increasing toward the periphery; (3) the parenchymal architecture — the functional lung parenchyma composed of alveolar tissue supported by a connective tissue stroma, organized into lobules supplied by terminal bronchioles; (4) the vascular supply — dual blood supply via bronchial arteries (systemic, nutrient supply from the aorta) and pulmonary arteries (gas exchange, deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle), with pulmonary veins draining oxygenated blood to the left atrium; (5) the pleural covering — each lung is enveloped by visceral pleura that extends into the fissures, continuous at the hilum with parietal pleura lining the thoracic cavity. It persists as a maintained anatomical landmark in pulmonology, thoracic surgery, radiology, and respiratory medicine. e.g.: the lung as described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; chest CT showing right lower lobe consolidation in community-acquired pneumonia; wedge resection specimen of pulmonary nodule examined on histology per WHO classification of lung tumors | not: the pleura (the serous membrane enclosing the lung, a distinct structure); the bronchus (the major airway conducting air into the lung, a proximal structure) [formal: pulmon | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
